answer.rationale: With the contract expiring in 14 days and the line running at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer, any vendor switch (memory_c2) carries onboarding and ramp risk that could tip delivery into shortfall—unacceptable given the primary objective of not increasing delivery risk. Memory_c4 shows that benchmarking and renegotiating with the incumbent at renewal previously recovered real margin and improved payment terms without disrupting supply, and memory_c1/c6 confirm the incumbent relationship preserves integration stability and can still yield volume-based cost reductions. Given the 18% cost mandate must be pursued without destabilizing an already-tight line, negotiating harder terms with the incumbent (using market benchmarks and possibly a longer-term volume commitment per c6) is the lowest-risk path to real savings this cycle. I verified c4 and c2 to confirm the actual negotiation outcomes and the true risk profile of the low-cost switch before ruling it out. This is applied at full contract scale since it's the primary supply agreement covering all committed volume, not a partial trial. Full achievement of the 18% target via negotiation alone is not guaranteed, so that residual cost-risk is flagged for next cycle's review alongside continued monitoring of second-sourcing options.
